title: Transformation of the office: territorial behaviour and place attachment in shared desk design
research_question: The purpose of this paper is to present an environmental psychological case study regarding an office design change. The authors examined the development of participants' territorial behaviour and place attachment.

participants.description: Employees from a large multinational company in Hungary, Europe, across four different functional areas. Average age 37.59 years (SD = 7.44), 45.11% male, 54.89% female.
participants.recruitment: Online questionnaire delivered by organizational contact person to employees of participating groups. Participation was anonymous and voluntary.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Office design change: choice between classic open office with permanent workstation or shared desk with one-day-a-week home office possibility.

measures.instrument: Hungarian version of Territorial Behaviour Questionnaire (Brown, 2009; Frankó, 2019), 7-point Likert scale
Hungarian version of Territorial Behaviour Questionnaire (Brown, 2009; Frankó, 2019), 7-point Likert scale

Hungarian version of Workplace Attachment Scale (Scrima, 2015; Rioux, 2006; Frankó and Dúll, 2018), 5-point Likert scale
Workstation Attachment Scale (Frankó and Dúll, 2018), 5-point Likert scale (adapted from Workplace Attachment Scale)

measures.construct: General experiences, space use habits, benefits, disadvantages, social relations, home office experiences

findings.mechanism: Workstation attachment explains 37% of the value of workplace attachment, suggesting a nested relationship where workstation attachment is a smaller transactional unit within the office system.

mechanisms: Loss of permanent workstation reduces opportunities for personalization.
Newly depersonalized environment might implicitly pressure employees to reduce personalization to avoid being perceived as an 'out-group' member.
Online booking systems for shared desks may clarify territorial conditions, potentially reducing the need for defensive territorial behaviors.
Organizational culture or implicit/explicit policies might prevent employees from engaging in defensive territorial actions.
The ability for employees to choose their workstation setup (permanent vs. shared) may have contributed to the stability of overall workplace attachment.
Workstation attachment is a smaller, nested transactional unit within workplace attachment.
moderators: Individual choice (to stay in classic open office or switch to shared desk)
implementation_implications: Office redesign is a psychological issue, not just economic or interior design.
Assurance of clear territorial conditions is a basic need for employees.
Design changes cause disruption and can lead to decreased satisfaction.
Crucial to create opportunities for identity-oriented marking (personalization) even in flexible offices, possibly through participatory planning or dedicated team rooms.
Placement of personal lockers is useful for securing belongings and resolving territorial conflicts, but should not be fixed to shared tables.
Allowing daily personalization (even with clean desk policy) provides a sense of security.
Personalization is essential for maintaining place attachment; its absence can reclassify office space as a secondary territory, leading to looser connections to team/organization.
Desk booking systems are important for control-oriented marking in virtual space, providing security and aiding self-regulation.
HR's role is essential to identify reasons for lack of defensive behavior (basic satisfaction vs. fear of retaliation).
Psychological ownership can develop for temporarily used workstations, making control over access essential.
The goal is to create the most functional person-physical environment-organization fit, considering employee needs, expectations, and psychological specialties of workplace designs.
Fostering efficient space use is an HR issue, achievable through adequate policies, educational programs, and community managers.
Free choice and employee autonomy are key for successful implementation of new office designs.

key_stats: Before intervention: 66 own workstation, 0 no workstation

Six-month follow-up: 64 no workstation, 33 own workstation

limitations: Methodological difficulties due to organizational contact (recruitment difficulties).
Logistical issues associated with design implementation.
Relatively low sample size for longitudinal analysis, necessitating independent sample tests.
Quasi-experimental design: no influence on the size and randomness of subgroups.
Questionnaire for control-oriented marking was incomplete as it did not capture virtual manifestations (e.g., booking system).
Lack of information to fully explain the absence of defensive behaviors (could be due to booking system or organizational culture preventing such actions).

paper_metadata.title: Transformation of the office: territorial behaviour and place attachment in shared desk design
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Transformation of the office: territorial behaviour and place attachment in shared desk design
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract:
Purpose
The purpose of this paper is to present an environmental psychological case study regarding an office design change. The employees of the researched company had the chance to decide whether to stay in the classic open office set-up or to switch to a shared desk supplemented by a one-day-a-week home office possibility. The authors examined the development of participants’ territorial behaviour and place attachment.


Design/methodology/approach
The given organizational situation is a quasi-experimental design; the variables were examined via questionnaire in a longitudinal model. Quantitative measurement was supplemented with focus group discussions.


Findings
The degree of personalization (a type of territorial behaviour) decreased significantly not only among those who lost their permanent workstations – as we expected – but also in the entire population. Workplace attachment stagnated for the entire population, but workstation attachment showed a significant decrease among those who switched to the shared desk.


Research limitations/implications
The limitations and the advantages are also followed by the nature of a case study: high ecological validity with relatively low sample size.


Practical implications
Redesigning an office is never just an economic or interior design issue, but a psychological one. This paper provides practical environmental psychological insights into implementing office designs without permanent individual workstations.


Originality/value
This paper presents the environmental psychological background of shared desk design implementation. The authors point out the significance of repressing personalization behaviour and as per the authors’ knowledge, they are the first to introduce the concept of workstation attachment.
